title: Mud and spit (John 9:1–12)
hook: who sinned, this man or his parents? neither; he makes clay and says go wash

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sentence carved in stone, and its quieter first half: if ye continue in my word. Your line was the truth shall make you free. Did you say your true thing? Day six hundred seventeen.

When something terrible happens, people reach for a reason. Somebody must have done something. A diagnosis, an accident, a child born with a disability, and the question comes, out loud or whispered: what did they do to deserve this? It's an old question. Jesus and his friends are walking along, and they pass a man who has been blind since birth. And the disciples, without even lowering their voices, turn him into a theology problem. "Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" The man can hear them.

The disciples give Jesus two choices. Either the man sinned, somehow, or his parents did. Jesus refuses both. "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." Neither. The blindness isn't a punishment. Christians have wrestled with the second half of that verse. Does it mean God made him blind just to make a point? Some readers answer by moving the full stop: neither this man sinned nor his parents. Period. Then: so that the works of God may be shown, we must work while it is day. Read that way, Jesus doesn't explain the blindness. He moves straight from blame to work. Then he does something earthy. "He spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay." Mud and spit. Not a word from a distance this time, like with the official's son. Touch. Some early Christian writers saw an echo of Genesis, where God forms the first human from the dust of the ground. Then: "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.)" The man has to walk there, still blind, mud on his face, through the streets of Jerusalem. "He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing." A handful of words for a whole new life. And the pool is real. Workers repairing a pipe in Jerusalem uncovered stone steps of a large pool from Jesus's time, which archaeologists identify as Siloam.
screen: `MUD AND SPIT, LIKE DUST IN EDEN.`
then, large: `NEITHER HATH THIS MAN SINNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop blaming someone's pain. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is suffering. A friend, a stranger in the news, maybe yourself. Notice if somewhere in you there's a quiet explanation. They should have known. They brought it on themselves. I must deserve this. You don't have to argue with it. Just notice it, and set it down. Then ask the question Jesus moved to instead: what work could I do here? A call, a meal, a ride, a kind word. If you pray, you can hold that person before God without explanations. If you don't, just hold them with care. The bell holds the time.
Siloam. The pool where Jesus sent a man born blind to wash off the clay, which John says means Sent.
Your line: neither sinned. Today, when you hear someone blame a person for their own pain, or catch yourself doing it, skip the reason and look for the work. Day six hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Christians often read this chapter in Lent, and many churches connect the washing in Siloam with baptism, which early Christians sometimes called illumination.

original.note: Greek form of Hebrew Shiloach. John translates it himself: Sent.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle story with a strange method.
what it means: Jesus refuses to blame anyone for the man's blindness, then heals him with mud, touch and a walk to the pool.
what a scholar hears: without punctuation, verses 3–4 can be read as moving straight from "neither sinned" to "we must work," and a pool identified as Siloam has been uncovered in Jerusalem.

notes: The alternative punctuation of John 9:3–4 is a known proposal; confirm it is fairly described as what 'some readers' do.
The Genesis 2:7 echo is made by Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.15.2) among others. Confirm citation.
Pool of Siloam discovered in 2004 during sewer repair work in the City of David; identified as the Second Temple period pool. Confirm.
Baptism called 'illumination' (photismos) in early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr (First Apology 61). Confirm for howItsDone.
